tagline.text: Body-paint dance revives Leyte's tattooed warriors

location.label: Location
location.text: Tacloban City, Leyte (Leyte Sports Development Center and downtown)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Mid to late June (main event around June 27)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 days (up to 10 days if you include Balyuan)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–8,000 (1 night in Tacloban, food, local transport; excluding flights)

children.text: The Pintados-Kasadyaan Festival is Tacloban's signature celebration, reviving the tradition of the Visayan warriors the Spanish called "painted people" through body-painted dance. Santo Niño devotions and the festivals of Leyte's towns come together in one big June celebration.

"Pintados" is Visayan for "painted ones." When the Spanish reached the Visayas in the 16th century, they met natives with tattoos covering their faces and bodies and called them this; the word also appears in the 1668 writings of Father Ignacio Francisco Alcina. Tattoos marked tribal identity, social rank and deeds in battle, and the bravest warriors are said to have had the most. The festival revives this tradition with patterns painted on the skin instead of ink, and dancers covered in black body paint are the main spectacle.

The festival has two roots. One is the event begun by the Pintados Foundation, formed by Tacloban residents in 1986 to honor the Santo Niño (the Christ Child); the first festival was held on June 29, 1987. The other is the Kasadyaan Festival, created on May 12, 1996 by then Leyte governor Remedios Petilla to bring together celebrations from Leyte, Biliran, Samar and other areas; "kasadyaan" means "merriment" in Visayan. The two merged in 1998 into one festival lasting through June, and it is now often called Leyte's "Festival of Festivals." Before that there was the Sangyaw Festival, held from 1974, which faded around the 1986 EDSA Revolution and was later revived.

The story behind the Santo Niño devotion and the date is worth knowing. The Santo Niño feast was originally in January, like Aklan's Ati-Atihan and Cebu's Sinulog. But in 1888 an image being shipped from Manila to Leyte was lost at sea just as cholera struck Tacloban; it is said that the image was found by people of Mindoro and returned to Leyte on June 30, 1889, and the epidemic subsided. The Tacloban Santo Niño celebration then moved to late June, and the Pintados-Kasadyaan is held in line with it. Since its return in 2015 the main event has been set around June 27, with feast-day events following on June 29–30.

For Korean travelers it is not as famous as Sinulog or MassKara, but that means fewer tourists and a festival where local people are the stars. It could not be held in 2020–2021 because of COVID, and since then it has continued on a smaller scale or at changed venues. The schedule, program and number of participating towns change from year to year, so the safest plan is to check the latest announcements from Tacloban City Hall and the organizers.

The heart of the festival is the ritual dance competition. Dancers covered in black body paint and dressed as warriors dance to express the old warrior culture and beliefs. Judging follows set criteria, and winning groups receive awards and prize money.

"Pagrayhak" means "to celebrate joyfully" and refers to the street-dance parade. Each Leyte town brings its own festival in this Festival of Festivals procession, and you can see body-painted groups, indigenous music and presentations of ancient idol worship.

Well-known town festivals take part, such as Buyogan of Abuyog, Lingganay of Alangalang, Pasaka of Tanauan, Buraburon of Burauen and Sanggutan of Barugo. According to Wikipedia, the 2024 champion was Buyogan of Abuyog. Winners get the chance to represent Leyte in national contests such as Aliwan Festival and Sinulog.

Balyuan, usually held around June 18–20, reenacts the old exchange of Santo Niño images between Tacloban and Buscada in Basey, Samar. Around the 18th (June 16–18 depending on the year) a replica image goes to Buscada in a motorcade, and on the 20th it returns to Tacloban in a fluvial procession across Cancabato Bay. The nine-day novena begins from this day.

blocks.title: Masses at Santo Niño Parish Church

children.text: The festival is also a religious event. For nine days before the main event, novena Masses are held at the Santo Niño Parish Church, with a solemn Mass on the feast day. Between the dancing and parades you can see devotees praying before the image, a reminder that faith is the foundation of the festival.

Events include Bituon han Leyte, which picks the lead female dancer, Miss Pintados and Miss Teen Pintados, and Ginoong Leyte, which picks a male representative. In some years there are also sports, singing, photo and dance contests, trade fairs and concerts.

A "subiran" is, in Waray, a one-person sailboat with outriggers. The sailboat race is held in Leyte Gulf on the east side of San Juanico Strait, another face of the seafaring culture of Leyte. Confirm locally whether it is held each year.
Have breakfast at your hotel and pack only what you need. The venue gets crowded from late morning, so bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
Walk around the Santo Niño Parish Church area and watch the devotees pray. The area around the church is very crowded during the festival, so watch your belongings.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town. Buying snacks such as binagol and moron, Leyte specialties, helps during the wait.
Arrive early at the venue and find a spot. In some recent years the ritual dance competition has been held at the Leyte Sports Development Center, so confirm the location first.
When the competition ends, walk or take a tricycle before sunset. Roads get congested as the event ends.
Event times and venues change from year to year, so this schedule is only a reference flow for the day. Always check that year's official program.

The main event is in late June. Since its return in 2015 it has been set around June 27, and in 2025 it was also announced for June 27. The Santo Niño feast is on June 29–30 and Balyuan is usually around June 18–20 (the pre-Balyuan rite is June 16–18 depending on the year).
June is the start of the Philippine rainy season, so sudden showers are frequent. You may get wet at outdoor events, so bring a raincoat and leave a spare day for schedule changes and delays.

Hotels are concentrated in downtown Tacloban. One guide lists GV Hotel Tacloban and Z Pad Residences as budget, Go Hotels Tacloban and Tacloban Plaza Hotel as mid-range, and Hotel XYZ and Ironwood Hotel as upscale. Rooms fill quickly during the festival, so book early. The venues and the church are close to downtown, so a downtown hotel is convenient for getting around on foot.

It is a good time to enjoy Leyte specialties. Moron and binagol, sweet snacks made with glutinous rice, are popular souvenirs, and lechon and seafood restaurants are easy to find. Street vendors sometimes sell snacks during events, so eat with care about hygiene.
Event times and venues change each year. Before you leave, check the latest announcements from Tacloban City Hall or the festival organizers.
Arrive 1–2 hours before the main event to get a spot, and you can see the dancers up close.
It is an outdoor event with little shade. Bring a hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and water, and a raincoat for the rainy season.
Put your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch in case of June showers.
The patterns painted on the dancers' bodies are the festival's symbol. When taking photos, ask first with a nod or a word.
Carry only a small bag with your wallet and a copy of your passport, and leave valuables at your hotel.
Combine San Juanico Bridge and the MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial with the event to make a full day.
Book your return flight with plenty of time after the event ends.
The schedule, venue and scale can change from year to year, and in some years fewer towns take part so the program shrinks. Always check the latest announcements.
Watch for pickpockets in crowds at the venue and around the church.
June is the rainy season, and heavy rain can delay events or change the schedule.
June is the start of typhoon season in Philippine waters. Check weather forecasts and flight notices before you travel.
